Chapter 5: The Calculus of Ruling — Self-Interest and Policy Choices
Now that we’ve laid out the basics of political survival and the differences between systems, let’s dive into something even more revealing — how self-interest really drives the choices leaders make.
No matter what they say in public, leaders are almost always running the same mental calculation: what do I need to do to stay in power?
This calculation isn’t random. It’s shaped by one key thing — the size and makeup of their winning coalition.
In systems with a small coalition, leaders focus their energy on rewarding a tight circle of core supporters. Sometimes, that means making decisions that actually hurt the broader population, just to keep those few people happy.
But in systems where leaders rely on a much larger coalition, they need to widen their appeal. That usually leads to policies that are more inclusive — and benefit more people.
Take foreign aid, for example. We’d like to think it’s all about fighting poverty or helping countries develop. But in reality, aid often ends up being a tool for leaders to shore up their own position. Instead of reaching the people who need it most, aid money might be funneled to key supporters, used to buy loyalty, or even suppress dissent. The general public? They might not see much of that money at all. But the leader’s coalition gets stronger.
You’ll see the same logic in economic policy. In autocracies, leaders might restrict economic opportunities — not because it’s best for the country, but to keep potential rivals from gaining enough power to challenge them. In democracies, policies are often designed to win over swing voters or please powerful interest groups, rather than serve the whole population.
Let’s look at a few practical techniques leaders use:
They’ll use state resources to reward loyalists and punish anyone who threatens their power. They’ll design policies that maximize their own survival, not necessarily the public good. And they’ll tweak the rules and institutions to make it tougher for challengers to build a coalition of their own.
So why do leaders so often resist reforms that would clearly help the public? It’s simple. If opening up the economy or allowing free elections would put their power at risk, they’re not likely to do it — even if it means missing out on real improvements for everyone.
And this isn’t just about domestic policy. When leaders deal with foreign countries, the same logic applies. They might start wars, sign treaties, or form alliances — not just for the nation’s sake, but because of how it affects their own coalition. The public story might be about security or national interest, but behind the scenes, it’s usually all about survival.
Once you see things from this angle, a lot of decisions that seemed irrational or even immoral start to make more sense. Leaders aren’t necessarily cruel or incompetent — they’re just responding to the incentives built into the system. And as long as those incentives stay the same, so will their behavior.
Here’s the big takeaway: better governance isn’t just about finding better leaders. It’s about changing the rules of the game itself. If we can reform the system — maybe by changing the size or makeup of the winning coalition — we can create new incentives that actually encourage leaders to serve the public good. Until then, the logic of political survival will keep driving the choices of those in charge.
